Department of Mathematics, Technische Universität München, Boltzmannstraße 3, 85748 Garching b. München, Germanybastian.hilder@tum.de Institute of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, University of Hohenheim, Schloss Hohenheim 1, 70599 Stuttgart, Germanyjonas.jansen@uni-hohenheim.de

Slow-moving pattern interfaces in general directions for a two-dimensional Swift–Hohenberg-type equation

Jonas Jansen
Abstract

We rigorously prove the bifurcation of slow-moving pattern interfaces with general direction in a two-dimensional Swift–Hohenberg-type model close to a Turing instability for a large class of nonlinearities. These interfaces describe the invasion of stripe and hexagonal patterns into the spatially homogeneous state and model a possible mechanism for pattern formation, as observed in a wide range of real-world applications. For this, we develop a rigorous framework to establish the existence of such solutions using spatial dynamics and non-standard centre manifold theory. Our approach exploits geometric and algebraic structures generic to O⁡(2)\mathrm{O}(2)-symmetric pattern-forming systems near a Turing instability, and addresses fundamental technical challenges due to a non-uniform spectral gap around the imaginary axis, quadratic resonances induced by the hexagonal structure, and the high-dimensional phase space of the reduced equations.

Contents

1  Introduction

The formation of spatially regular structures is ubiquitous in natural systems and can be observed in hydrodynamic convection problems [Pea58, SH77], vegetation systems [Kla99, Mer18], biological and chemical systems [GM72, OS91], and engineering applications [CB95, Ban+19]. These spatial patterns typically arise when a spatially homogeneous state destabilises in response to a change in a system parameter. One of the most famous examples is the Turing instability [Tur52], where the spatially homogeneous state becomes unstable in a neighbourhood of a finite Fourier wave number, which leads to the formation of steady, spatially periodic structures such as hexagonal and stripe patterns. In applications, these spatial patterns typically arise in the wake of an invasion front, which facilitates the spatial transition from the pattern to the unstable homogeneous state, see Figure 1. These fronts can appear as radial invasion phenomena, in which the pattern spreads into the unstable state from an initial point defect [Bod+91], or as planar invasion fronts, in which the pattern and the unstable state are separated by a moving planar interface [NT95].

In this paper, we study the existence of two-dimensional, planar pattern interfaces close to a Turing instability. It is well known that the dynamics close to these instabilities are universal, and the emerging structures are independent of the specific application, cf. Section 1.1. Therefore, we analyse the existence of pattern interfaces in a semilinear Swift–Hohenberg-type equation

@t​u=L⁡(∇,�)​u+N⁡(u,D​u,D2​u,D3​u,#),L⁡(∇,�)​u=−(1+�)2​u+�​u\partial_{t}u=L(\nabla;\mu)u+N(u,Du,D^{2}u,D^{3}u;\vartheta),\qquad L(\nabla;\mu)u=-(1+\Delta)^{2}u+\mu u (1.1)

with u⁡(t,𝐱)∈ℝu(t,\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}, a set of parameters #∈�\vartheta\in\Theta, time t⩾0t\geqslant 0 and space 𝐱∈ℝ2\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. The classical Swift–Hohenberg equation with N⁡(u)=−u3N(u)=-u^{3} was first proposed as a model for the formation of thermally-driven convection cells in fluid applications [SH77]. The equation (1.1) undergoes a Turing instability at �=0\mu=0, that is, there exists a critical absolute wave number kc=1k_{c}=1, such that, for �>0\mu>0, solutions to the linearised equation of the form e�​t−i​𝐤⋅𝐱e^{\lambda t-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}} grow exponentially for |𝐤||\mathbf{k}| close to kck_{c} and decay otherwise, cf. Appendix A. Therefore, this is a prototypical model to study the dynamics close to such an instability. Planar pattern interfaces for a similar model with N⁡(u)=−�​|∇u|2−u3N(u)=-\beta|\nabla u|^{2}-u^{3} were first constructed in [Doe+03], where the authors obtained solutions travelling in x1x_{1}-direction under the assumption that |�|≪1|\beta|\ll 1.

Here, we develop a fully rigorous framework for two-dimensional pattern interfaces connecting periodic solutions on a hexagonal Fourier lattice and travelling in general directions 𝐝=(cos⁡(�),sin⁡(�))\mathbf{d}=(\cos(\theta),\sin(\theta)) satisfying cot⁡(�)∈3​ℚ\cot(\theta)\in\sqrt{3}\mathbb{Q} for a Swift–Hohenberg-type equation with a generic class of nonlinearities. The framework relies on a spatial-dynamics approach with a non-standard normal-form transformation and centre manifold reduction with a non-uniform spectral gap. Specifically, we address two fundamentally new mathematical obstacles: quadratic resonances inherent to the hexagonal lattice structure induce singular scalings in the normal-form analysis, and the insufficient gain of regularity in the front direction, which requires a functional-analytic framework using mixed-regularity Sobolev spaces. This approach reduces the construction of pattern interfaces to proving the existence of travelling fronts in a system of degenerate Ginzburg–Landau equations. Here, we prove the existence of selected heteroclinic orbits, which completes the fully rigorous construction of specific planar fronts. We refer to Section 1.4 for a detailed list of the main results.

While the specific analysis is restricted to (1.1), our framework applies much more broadly to generic rotational- and reflectional-invariant, semilinear pattern-forming systems close to a Turing instability. Indeed, wherever possible, we exploit generic geometric and algebraic properties of such systems in our analysis rather than relying on explicit computations.

The system (1.5) can formally be derived from (1.1), or, in fact, a general O⁡(n)\mathrm{O}(n)-symmetric pattern-forming system close to a Turing instability, through multiscale expansion. In spatially one-dimensional systems, or more generally, systems on an infinite cylinder, there is a well-developed justification theory, which shows that the resulting amplitude equation, the classical real Ginzburg–Landau equation, makes good predictions for the dynamics over a long time interval. Moreover, there are approximation results stating that any small solution will, to leading order, eventually be localised in Fourier space at the critical wave numbers, and the corresponding amplitudes are again determined by the one-dimensional amplitude equation. It is expected that these results directly extend to the two-dimensional case if the solution is sufficiently localised in Fourier space at the lattice points in �\Gamma and the nonlinearity satisfies the smallness condition in Assumption B. We refer to [SU17, Ch. 10] for a more detailed discussion of this topic.

1.2  Selected speeds and marginal stability analysis

As is typical for invasion phenomena into unstable states, our analysis yields a continuous family of fronts with different speeds for each direction. This raises the natural question: which front is selected, i.e., which front forms in the time-evolution problem starting from steep or step-like initial data? This question has attracted much attention recently, and for invading fronts in spatially one-dimensional reaction-diffusion equations where the spatially homogeneous invading state is exponentially stable, a robust framework for stability and front selection is available, see e.g. [AS22, AHS25]. In addition, there are recent advances in generalising this framework to steady pattern-forming fronts where the front is stationary in an appropriate co-moving frame, see [ACR26]. In contrast, the pattern interfaces constructed in this paper are non-steady as they describe a connection of two stationary patterns via a moving front. To the best of our knowledge, a rigorous framework is not available for such non-steady pattern-forming fronts, even in one spatial dimension, or spatially two-dimensional reaction-diffusion systems.

Although a rigorous framework is lacking, there are formal conjectures about front selection in situations where the front dynamics are determined by the linear behaviour about the unstable state, which are referred to as pulled fronts. Here, the conjectured selected front speed can be determined through the marginal stability conjecture, see e.g. [vSaa03] and [AHS25, Def. 6.8 and Conj. 6.9]. For this, one observes that the unstable state, when viewed in a moving reference frame, transitions from absolutely unstable to convectively unstable as the reference frame speed increases. That is, at low speeds, a perturbation of the unstable state will grow exponentially at each fixed point, while at high speeds it will decay exponentially at each fixed point. The marginal stability conjecture states that the selected speed is the one at which the system transitions from absolute to convective instability.

In practice, the conjectured selected speed is determined from the dispersion relation of the linearisation about the unstable state in a co-moving frame �=𝐱−𝐝​c​t\boldsymbol{\xi}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{d}ct, which is obtained by making an ansatz of the form u⁡(t,�)=e�​t+�⋅�u(t,\boldsymbol{\xi})=e^{\lambda t+\boldsymbol{\nu}\cdot\boldsymbol{\xi}} with �∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C} and �∈ℂ2\boldsymbol{\nu}\in\mathbb{C}^{2}. In our case, the resulting dispersion relation reads as

This is reflected by writing �=�​𝐝+i​k⟂​𝐝⟂\boldsymbol{\nu}=\nu\mathbf{d}+ik_{\perp}\mathbf{d}^{\perp} with �∈ℂ\nu\in\mathbb{C}, k⟂∈ℝk_{\perp}\in\mathbb{R}. 1.3  General strategies and main challenges

To construct the pattern interfaces, we use a spatial-dynamics approach, [Kir82], where an elliptic system is written as a dynamical system by interpreting a spatial variable as ’time’. This approach has been used successfully to construct, primarily one-dimensional, pattern interfaces [EW91, HS99, Doe+03, FH15, Hil20, Hil22, HJ25]. For this, we make the ansatz

The main challenge in the centre-manifold analysis is that ℒ~0\tilde{\mathcal{L}}^{0} has infinitely many, purely imaginary eigenvalues, which move away from the imaginary axis at different speeds for ">0\varepsilon>0, creating an "\varepsilon-dependent splitting between finitely many more-central and infinitely many less-central eigenvalues. Although a similar problem appeared in previous papers, see e.g. [HS99], in two-dimensional systems with a general class of quadratic nonlinearities, additional obstructions arise due to the resonance of the hexagonal lattice. Note that this condition is satisfied for �=0\theta=0 and �=�6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}.

The final step of the analysis is the derivation and analysis of the system of reduced equations on the centre manifold. As expected, this system is indeed given by the travelling-wave system (1.6) obtained from the amplitude system (1.5). Due to the high dimensionality of the reduced system, constructing heteroclinic orbits between equilibria is another main challenge, which we at least partially address in this paper.

1.4  Main results of the paper

We now summarise the main results and techniques of this paper. We show that

    for ">0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small, cot⁡(�)∈3​ℚ\cot(\theta)\in\sqrt{3}\mathbb{Q}, �0∈ℝ∖{0}\mu_{0}\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}, and c0>0c_{0}>0, the system (1.11) has a finite-dimensional, locally invariant centre manifold, which contains all small bounded solutions to (1.11) of size 𝒪⁡("3/4+�)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{3/4+\delta}) with 0<�<140<\delta<\tfrac{1}{4} and the reduced equations on the centre manifold are, to leading order, given by (1.6), see Theorem 3.10;

Remark 1.3.

We focus on the analysis for patterns, which are periodic with respect to a hexagonal lattice. However, the same analysis can also be done for square patterns, see Section 5. In fact, this case is less challenging since the corresponding Fourier lattice is non-resonant.

Remark 1.4.

We note that due to rotation and reflection symmetry, it is sufficient to consider directions with angle �∈[0,�6]\theta\in[0,\tfrac{\pi}{6}].

Spectral Analysis

The key insight for the spectral analysis is that the eigenvalues of ℒ~\tilde{\mathcal{L}} can be characterised through the linearisation of the Swift–Hohenberg equation (1.1), specifically, through roots of L"​(𝐝​�+i​ )+"​c0​�L^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{d}\lambda+i\boldsymbol{\gamma})+\varepsilon c_{0}\lambda and their multiplicity, cf. Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2. This is not a new observation and has been pointed out, for example, in [AM95]. For two-dimensional fronts, this allows for a direct geometric interpretation: if the line ` :={ +𝐝​�:�∈ℝ}\ell_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}:=\{\boldsymbol{\gamma}+\mathbf{d}\lambda\,:\,\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\} intersects the unit circle, the corresponding ℒ~0​( )\tilde{\mathcal{L}}^{0}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}) has only purely imaginary eigenvalues with imaginary parts given by the distance between the intersection points and \boldsymbol{\gamma}, see Figure 5. In particular, the critical Fourier modes yield eigenvalues at zero. Moreover, if ` \ell_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} has no intersection points, the eigenvalues of ℒ~0​( )\tilde{\mathcal{L}}^{0}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}) have real part with absolute value given by the minimal distance of ` \ell_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} to the circle. In particular, this shows that there is a spectral gap around the imaginary axis for "=0\varepsilon=0 if and only if the lattice is periodic in direction 𝐝\mathbf{d}, which is equivalent to the condition cot⁡(�)∈3​ℚ\cot(\theta)\in\sqrt{3}\mathbb{Q}. In addition to the value of the eigenvalues, the geometric picture also characterises their algebraic multiplicity, which is given by the multiplicity of the root of �↦L0​(𝐝​�+i​ )\lambda\mapsto L^{0}(\mathbf{d}\lambda+i\boldsymbol{\gamma}). So, the eigenvalues belong to two Jordan blocks of size two if the line ` \ell_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} has two or zero intersections with the circle or a Jordan block of size four if ` \ell_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} is tangent to the circle, using the generic structure of the Turing instability.

For ">0\varepsilon>0, the eigenvalues on the imaginary axis depart at different speeds in "\varepsilon. Indeed, any eigenvalues emerging from zero have real part 𝒪⁡(")\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) and any eigenvalues emerging from a non-zero point on the imaginary axis have real part 𝒪⁡(")\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\varepsilon}). The only exception is the case �=�6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}, where there are Jordan blocks of size four at zero corresponding to =±𝐤2\boldsymbol{\gamma}=\pm\mathbf{k}_{2} and which split into one eigenvalue with real part 𝒪⁡(")\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) and three eigenvalues with real part 𝒪⁡("1/3)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{1/3}). Again, this is a generic effect, since the system is close to a (rotation-symmetric) Turing instability, cf. Appendix A.

The spectral picture for ">0\varepsilon>0 is thus as follows: there are finitely many more-central eigenvalues with real part 𝒪⁡(")\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon), and the remaining eigenvalues split into less-central eigenvalues with real part 𝒪⁡(")\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\varepsilon}) and hyperbolic eigenvalues.

Centre manifold reduction

The next step is to prove that there is a locally invariant centre manifold associated with the finitely many more-central eigenvalues. As discussed above, the main obstruction is the non-uniform spectral gap. Therefore, one has to carefully track the dependence on "\varepsilon throughout the proof of the centre manifold theorem. This has been done before, mainly for systems with one unbounded spatial direction, see e.g. [HS99], and the main steps are as follows: first, we split the unknown variable into a more-central, less-central, and hyperbolic part. Second, we introduce rescaled variables, where the more-central, less-central, and hyperbolic parts are rescaled with suitable fractional powers of "\varepsilon, and which allow us to determine the size of the centre manifold.

The third step is then to show that the resulting rescaled system has a centre manifold of size 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1). For this, we first apply a normal-form transformation to remove problematic quadratic nonlinear terms with a singular scaling in "\varepsilon. Here, new effects emerge in the two-dimensional case since the typical non-resonance condition in the normal-form analysis, cf. [GH83, Sec. 3.3], is not satisfied uniformly in "\varepsilon. Nevertheless, it is possible to obtain a near-identity normal-form transformation, cf. (3.9) and Lemma 3.5 by exploiting the "\sqrt{\varepsilon}-behaviour of the less-central eigenvalues. The second step is to obtain sufficient semigroup estimates, cf. Lemma 3.9, and to construct a centre manifold using the usual fixed-point construction. Here, the main obstruction in two dimensions is that the semigroups are analytic in 𝐝⟂\mathbf{d}^{\perp}-direction, but do not gain enough regularity in 𝐝\mathbf{d}-direction to compensate for more than one derivative in 𝐝\mathbf{d}-direction. Therefore, the fact that the nonlinearities of the spatial-dynamics system (1.11) only contain 𝐝⟂\mathbf{d}^{\perp}-derivatives becomes crucial. To exploit this structure, we perform the fixed-point argument in periodic Sobolev spaces with mixed dominating smoothness, see (3.1). Carefully tracking the dependence on "\varepsilon then yields a centre manifold of size 𝒪⁡("3/4+�)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{3/4+\delta}) for �∈(0,14)\delta\in(0,\tfrac{1}{4}), cf. Theorem 3.10. This specifically is large enough to contain solutions to (1.1) of size "\varepsilon, which covers the pattern-dynamics near onset, cf. (1.4). Notably, the resulting centre manifold is smaller than in the one-dimensional case, cf. [HS99], where the size is of order "2/3+�\varepsilon^{2/3+\delta}. This difference originates directly from the degenerate normal-form transformation, which yields an additional condition 2​�−12>12\beta-\tfrac{1}{2}>1 from the Lipschitz constant of the less-central nonlinearity, cf. Lemma 3.7, which is not present in the one-dimensional case.

On the centre manifold, we then derive the reduced equation

4​(𝐝⋅𝐤1)2​@�2​A1+c0​@�​A1+�0​A1+�2​A¯2​A¯3+(K0​|A1|2+K2​(|A2|2+|A3|2))​A1+𝒪⁡(")=0,4​(𝐝⋅𝐤2)2​@�2​A2+c0​@�​A2+�0​A2+�2​A¯1​A¯3+(K0​|A2|2+K2​(|A1|2+|A3|2))​A2+𝒪⁡(")=0,4​(𝐝⋅𝐤3)2​@�2​A3+c0​@�​A3+�0​A3+�2​A¯1​A¯2+(K0​|A3|2+K2​(|A1|2+|A2|2))​A3+𝒪⁡(")=0,\begin{split}4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{1})^{2}\partial_{\Xi}^{2}A_{1}+c_{0}\partial_{\Xi}A_{1}+\mu_{0}A_{1}+\beta_{2}\bar{A}_{2}\bar{A}_{3}+(K_{0}|A_{1}|^{2}+K_{2}(|A_{2}|^{2}+|A_{3}|^{2}))A_{1}+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)&=0,\\ 4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{2})^{2}\partial_{\Xi}^{2}A_{2}+c_{0}\partial_{\Xi}A_{2}+\mu_{0}A_{2}+\beta_{2}\bar{A}_{1}\bar{A}_{3}+(K_{0}|A_{2}|^{2}+K_{2}(|A_{1}|^{2}+|A_{3}|^{2}))A_{2}+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)&=0,\\ 4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{3})^{2}\partial_{\Xi}^{2}A_{3}+c_{0}\partial_{\Xi}A_{3}+\mu_{0}A_{3}+\beta_{2}\bar{A}_{1}\bar{A}_{2}+(K_{0}|A_{3}|^{2}+K_{2}(|A_{1}|^{2}+|A_{2}|^{2}))A_{3}+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)&=0,\end{split} (1.12)

which in particular agrees to leading order with the travelling-wave amplitude equations (1.6). Although the derivation is mostly standard, we introduce a systematic change of variables exploiting the Jordan-block structure at "=0\varepsilon=0, see (3.25). This agrees with the ad-hoc change of variables used, for example, in [EW91], but makes the connection to the algebraic structure of the eigenvalues more transparent.

Note that there are two special cases, which require separate treatment. The first case is �=�6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}. As discussed above, in this case, ℒ~0​(±𝐤2)\tilde{\mathcal{L}}^{0}(\pm\mathbf{k}_{2}) has an eigenvalue at zero corresponding to a Jordan block of size four, which splits into one more-central and three less-central eigenvalues. Therefore, in contrast to the generic case �≠�6\theta\neq\tfrac{\pi}{6}, we cannot define uniformly bounded projections separating the more-central and less-central eigenvalues. However, it is still possible to construct a centre manifold of the same size, cf. Section 3.5, by defining non-normalised ’projection-like’ maps, see (3.34), which still map into the relevant eigenspace. With this, the rest of the proof works the same as in the generic-angle case and the reduced equations on the centre manifold are again given by (1.12) with 𝐝⋅𝐤2=0\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{2}=0.

The second case is c0=ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{0}=c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}), where

ccrit​(𝐤j):=4​|𝐝⋅𝐤j|​�0c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}):=4|\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{j}|\sqrt{\mu_{0}} (1.13)

Notably, it can be obtained from (1.8) where the transverse wave number k⟂k_{\perp} is given by 𝐝⟂⋅𝐤j\mathbf{d}^{\perp}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{j}. In the spectral analysis, this speed yields a different "\varepsilon-expansion of the more-central eigenvalues. Specifically, for c0≠ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{0}\neq c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}) for all j=1,2,3j=1,2,3, the more-central eigenvalues coming from ℒ~"​(𝐤j)\tilde{\mathcal{L}}^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{k}_{j}) split at leading order "\varepsilon for all j=1,2,3j=1,2,3. In contrast, for c0=ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{0}=c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}) for fixed j=1,2,3j=1,2,3 the leading-order behaviour of the more-central eigenvalues from ℒ~"​(𝐤j)\tilde{\mathcal{L}}^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{k}_{j}) is the same and they only split at order "3/2\varepsilon^{3/2}. While this does not affect the construction of the centre manifold, since the more-central eigenvalues still are of order "\varepsilon, it changes the derivation of the reduced equations, see Section 3.6. However, the resulting leading-order system on the centre manifold is still (1.6). Indeed, this is expected since the derivation of the amplitude system (1.5) is done in the stationary frame. Nevertheless, as pointed out in Section 4.1.3, the dynamics of the reduced equation still change when c0c_{0} passes through ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}) for some j=1,2,3j=1,2,3.

Dynamics of reduced equations and pattern interfaces

Finally, we analyse the dynamics of the reduced system (1.12) on the centre manifold. For this, we restrict the corresponding twelve-dimensional (note the complex conjugate equations) first-order system to the invariant, six-dimensional subspace of real-valued solutions. For the special direction �=0\theta=0, there is an additional four-dimensional invariant subspace, see [Doe+03]. However, to deal with general directions, we analyse the full six-dimensional system. We first collect non-trivial equilibria, which correspond to planar patterns in (1.1) and which can be obtained using standard results from equivariant bifurcation theory. To analyse their stability, we establish a rigorous relation between the temporal stability of an equilibrium as a stationary state in the Ginzburg–Landau system (1.5) without diffusion, and the stability in the spatial dynamics system on the centre manifold, see Lemma 4.4. Specifically, temporally fully unstable equilibria are stable in the reduced equation on the centre manifold, and temporally stable equilibria are saddles with an even splitting between stable and unstable directions. In particular, this implies that for �0>0\mu_{0}>0, the trivial equilibrium is stable. While this characterisation was previously noted, see e.g. [Doe+03], to the best of our knowledge, a rigorous proof is not available in the literature. Moreover, we discuss that the result also applies to reaction-diffusion systems when the linearisation about an equilibrium is symmetric; otherwise, it might fail, see Remark 4.6.

To obtain heteroclinic orbits, we use that the leading-order first-order system has a strictly decreasing Lyapunov function, see (4.14). Restricting to the case �0>0\mu_{0}>0, c0>0c_{0}>0, K0<0K_{0}<0 and K2<−K02K_{2}<-\tfrac{K_{0}}{2}, we use this to prove the existence of heteroclinic orbits between the non-trivial equilibrium with lowest energy and the (stable) trivial equilibrium, see Theorem 4.10 for the case �≠�6\theta\neq\tfrac{\pi}{6}. The proof relies on constructing an appropriate bounded trapping region around the trivial equilibrium using the Lyapunov function. Their persistence then follows using the transverse intersection of stable and unstable manifolds, see Theorem 4.12. Finally, using fast-slow analysis, we show that these orbits converge to a heteroclinic orbit connecting the same patterns along a sequence of angles �\theta satisfying cot⁡(�)∈3​ℚ\cot(\theta)\in\sqrt{3}\mathbb{Q} and converging to �6\tfrac{\pi}{6}. Similarly, the fast-moving pattern interfaces obtained in [HJ25] can be recovered in the limit c0→∞c_{0}\to\infty as expected.

In addition to the rigorous analysis, we find heteroclinic orbits using a numerical shooting algorithm, which yields orbits connecting the other non-trivial equilibrium to the trivial state, see Figures 1 and 12 for the corresponding planar interfaces. In particular, we find orbits from up-hexagons to the trivial state, which pass close to the roll waves and thus correspond to a two-stage invasion described in Section 1.2 where the primary and secondary invasion fronts have the same speed, see Figure 12c.

1.5  Related results

We now discuss related results. As mentioned above, the existence of pattern interfaces using spatial dynamics and centre manifold theory is well-known for systems in an infinite cylinder. Specifically, they have been constructed for the one-dimensional Swift–Hohenberg equation [EW91], the Taylor–Couette problem [HS99], and a non-local reaction-diffusion system [FH15]. In the case of a Turing(–Hopf) instability with additional conservation law, which for example appears in the Bénard–Marangoni problem, one-dimensional pattern interfaces have been found in phenomenological models [Hil20, Hil22]. Recently, the existence, stability, and selection of related (steady) front solutions have also been studied in the FitzHugh–Nagumo system [Ave+25, ACR26].

In systems with two unbounded spatial directions, results are sparser. Besides the existence result for planar pattern interfaces in [Doe+03], much attention has been focused on stationary interfaces between differently oriented roll waves, which are also known as grain boundary or domain walls. Their existence has been obtained for a two-dimensional Swift–Hohenberg equation [HS07, HS12] and, more recently, for the Rayleigh–Bénard problem [HI21, HI22, BHI23, Ioo25, Ioo26]. While these results are restricted to semilinear systems, fast-moving pattern interfaces with c=𝒪⁡(1)c=\mathcal{O}(1) have recently been obtained in a quasilinear asymptotic thin-film model for the Bénard–Marangoni problem [HJ25]. We expect that the generic approach of this paper can also be transferred to construct slow-moving pattern interfaces in these models. However, there are substantial additional difficulties which we discuss in more detail in Section 6.

All of the previously mentioned results used a spatial-dynamics approach to obtain the existence of pattern interfaces. This approach does not directly translate to systems that exhibit multiple, simultaneous pattern-forming instabilities which occur at resonant wave numbers. Here, difficulties arise from additional interactions of the critical modes. For these systems, the existence of solutions in one spatial dimension that are close to pattern interfaces at least on a long time interval has been established using modulation theory [Gau+21, HK25].

The study of steady localised solutions to pattern-forming systems has received much interest in recent years, and we refer to [BHL25] for a recent overview. Many of these results rely on numerical continuation methods, for example, obtained using pde2path [Uec21], see [UW14] for an application. While these references mainly consider stationary solutions and the existence of radial front solutions remains a largely open question, we highlight the recent derivation of radial amplitude equations [HL24].

Numerical continuation methods in combination with far-field-core decompositions have also been used recently to study the behaviour of invading one-dimensional pattern interfaces beyond onset [LGR25].

1.6  Outline of the paper

The paper is structured as follows: In Section 2, we perform a spectral analysis of the linearity in the spatial-dynamics system (1.11) by first analysing the spectrum for "=0\varepsilon=0, and then characterising the behaviour of the eigenvalues for ">0\varepsilon>0.

In Section 3, we prove a centre manifold theorem for the spatial-dynamics system (1.11) and derive the reduced equations. For this, we first introduce an appropriate functional-analytic setup based on mixed-regularity Sobolev spaces and then perform a normal-form analysis in a rescaled system. Then, we prove the necessary bounds on the semigroups to obtain a sufficiently large centre manifold with a standard fixed-point argument. In the analysis, we first consider the generic case �≠�6\theta\neq\tfrac{\pi}{6} and c0≠ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{0}\neq c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}). Then, we provide a proof of the centre manifold theorem in the special case �=�6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}, and a derivation of the reduced equation in the case c0=ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{0}=c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}) separately.

Section 4 then contains the analysis of the dynamics of the reduced equations on the centre manifold. Here, we first discuss the equilibria which correspond to planar patterns in (1.1), and characterise their stability. Afterwards, we prove the existence of persistent heteroclinic orbits and use this to establish the existence of slow-moving pattern interfaces in (1.1), see Theorem 4.14.

In Section 5, we discuss how our results transfer from the hexagonal lattice case to the square lattice case. We conclude the main body of the paper by discussing related questions in Section 6. In Appendix A, we then provide a detailed discussion of how the spectral results apply more generally to generic, rotation-invariant pattern-forming systems close to a Turing instability. Finally, Appendix B contains numerical results on the selected front speed.

2  Spectral analysis

We now analyse the spectrum of the linear part of (1.11). Although the calculations are done for the linear operator given by the Swift–Hohenberg-type equation (1.1), the results are fully generic for rotationally symmetric pattern-forming systems close to a Turing instability, albeit with more involved notation. We outline this in detail in Appendix A. 3  Centre manifold theory and reduced equations

We now establish a centre manifold theorem following the analysis in [HS99] and pay particular attention to the size of the centre manifold. We first restrict to the case cot⁡(�)∈3​ℚ\cot(\theta)\in\sqrt{3}\mathbb{Q} with �≠�6\theta\neq\tfrac{\pi}{6}, where the more-central eigenvalues belong to Jordan blocks at zero of size 2. We then discuss the extension to the case �=�6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}, when there are more-central eigenvalues belonging to a Jordan block of size 4 in Section 3.5. The derivation of the reduced equations in the case c0=ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{0}=c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}) is done in Section 3.6.

The analysis is split into different steps: first, we define the necessary projections onto the more-central, less-central, and hyperbolic parts and introduce rescaled variables by using different rescalings for the different parts of the solution. These rescaled variables make the "\varepsilon-dependence in the centre manifold analysis explicit and allow us to show that the centre manifold is indeed large enough to contain interesting solutions. Next, we perform a normal-form analysis to remove the terms with the lowest-order scaling in "\varepsilon. Finally, we show that we can close a fixed-point argument to obtain a centre manifold, which is of size 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) in the rescaled variables. Returning to the original variables then yields a centre manifold which is sufficiently large to contain the relevant solutions.

3.1  Functional analytic set-up and projections

We start by introducing the proper function spaces to perform the centre manifold analysis. For the following analysis, we need additional notation to distinguish regularity in 𝐝\mathbf{d}-direction and 𝐝⟂\mathbf{d}^{\perp}-direction. The reason is that the real part of the eigenvalues of ℒ~"\tilde{\mathcal{L}}^{\varepsilon} emerging from the imaginary axis only behaves like ("​|𝐝⋅ |)1/4(\varepsilon|\mathbf{d}\cdot\boldsymbol{\gamma}|)^{1/4} as |𝐝⋅ |→∞|\mathbf{d}\cdot\boldsymbol{\gamma}|\rightarrow\infty and |𝐝⟂⋅ |<C|\mathbf{d}^{\perp}\cdot\boldsymbol{\gamma}|<C. Therefore, we cannot expect that the corresponding stable and unstable semigroups can compensate for the loss of more than one derivative in 𝐝\mathbf{d}-direction. However, it turns out that this is not necessary as the spatial-dynamics formulation (1.11) is designed so that only Fourier multipliers in 𝐝⟂⋅ \mathbf{d}^{\perp}\cdot\boldsymbol{\gamma} occur in the nonlinearity and it therefore suffices to gain regularity in 𝐝⟂\mathbf{d}^{\perp}-direction. This motivates the following definitions. [Han10]. 3.2  The rescaled system and normal-form analysis

We now construct a centre manifold by following the general strategy in [HS99]: First, we split the variables into a more-central, less-central, and hyperbolic part. The main idea for quantifying the "\varepsilon-dependence is to introduce rescaled variables that use different "\varepsilon-rescalings for the more-central part compared to the less-central and hyperbolic parts. We then prove that the resulting rescaled system has a centre manifold of size 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1), and therefore, that the "\varepsilon-dependence for the centre manifold in the original system is fully characterised by the rescaling. The construction follows the standard approach, except for one main obstruction: the quadratic terms generate nonlinear contributions which prevent a direct fixed-point construction. However, these can be handled by invoking Assumption B and performing an "\varepsilon-dependent normal-form transformation.

Following the standard construction [HI11], we aim to obtain a centre manifold as a fixed point of the variation of constants formula in exponentially weighted spaces, see (3.17). This requires estimating the product of a bound on the semigroups generated by 𝒫j"​ℒ~"\mathcal{P}_{j}^{\varepsilon}\tilde{\mathcal{L}}^{\varepsilon} and the Lipschitz constant of the projected nonlinearities locally around W≡0W\equiv 0. Since the nonlinearities are polynomials, they are locally Lipschitz with a local Lipschitz constant of the order of the corresponding "\varepsilon-scaling. If �≠�6\theta\neq\tfrac{\pi}{6}, the "\varepsilon-scaling of the semigroup bounds is inherited from the spectral behaviour, that is, the semigroups generated by ℒ~m​c"\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{mc}^{\varepsilon} and ℒ~l​c"\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon} scale like "−1\varepsilon^{-1} and the semigroup generated by ℒ~h"\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{h}^{\varepsilon} is bounded independent of "\varepsilon, see Lemma 3.8 for more details. Note that although the eigenvalues of ℒ~l​c"\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon} have real parts of order "\sqrt{\varepsilon}, it still generates a scaling of "−1\varepsilon^{-1} since the eigenvalues appear as Jordan blocks on the imaginary axis at "=0\varepsilon=0, which split into stable and unstable eigenvalues. The case �=�6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6} is more complicated and will be discussed later, see Section 3.5. However, it turns out that the relevant nonlinearities are the same.

This allows us to identify problematic nonlinearities in (3.8), which generate singular terms in "\varepsilon in the fixed-point argument. In the more-central equation, the only problematic nonlinearity is "�​𝒫m​c"​( )​𝒩^2​(W ^m​c, ,#)\varepsilon^{\beta}\mathcal{P}_{mc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma})\hat{\mathcal{N}}_{2}(\underaccent{\vphantom{W}\smash{\raisebox{1.59735pt}{\kern 0.0pt\rule{5.58054pt}{0.6pt}}}}{\hat{W}}_{mc};\boldsymbol{\gamma},\vartheta) since 0<�<1< 0<\beta<1<\gamma. In contrast to the one-dimensional case [HS99] and the square case discussed in Section 5, this term is in general non-zero due to the resonance of the hexagonal lattice. Therefore, we need the additional smallness Assumption B to guarantee that this term gains an additional "\varepsilon and can be handled in the fixed-point argument. In the less-central equation, the problematic terms are "2​�− 𝒫h"( )𝒩^2(W ^m​c; ,#)\varepsilon^{2\beta-\gamma}\mathcal{P}_{h}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma})\hat{\mathcal{N}}_{2}(\underaccent{\vphantom{W}\smash{\raisebox{1.59735pt}{\kern 0.0pt\rule{5.58054pt}{0.6pt}}}}{\hat{W}}_{mc};\boldsymbol{\gamma},\vartheta) and "�​𝒫l​c"​( )​𝒩^2​(W ^m​c,W ^l​c+W ^h, ,#)\varepsilon^{\beta}\mathcal{P}_{lc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma})\hat{\mathcal{N}}_{2}(\underaccent{\vphantom{W}\smash{\raisebox{1.59735pt}{\kern 0.0pt\rule{5.58054pt}{0.6pt}}}}{\hat{W}}_{mc},\underaccent{\vphantom{W}\smash{\raisebox{1.59735pt}{\kern 0.0pt\rule{5.58054pt}{0.6pt}}}}{\hat{W}}_{lc}+\underaccent{\vphantom{W}\smash{\raisebox{1.59735pt}{\kern 0.0pt\rule{5.58054pt}{0.6pt}}}}{\hat{W}}_{h};\boldsymbol{\gamma},\vartheta), where we point out that 2​�− <12\beta-\gamma<1 due to �<1< <2\beta<1<\gamma<2. As in [HS99], we show that there is a normal-form transformation to remove these terms. Note that, in contrast to [HS99], the resonances of the hexagonal lattice cause additional obstructions. However, we still obtain a uniformly bounded, near-identity transformation under the additional, non-restrictive assumption �>12\beta>\tfrac{1}{2}, cf. Lemma 3.5. Finally, since the semigroup generated in the hyperbolic equation is uniformly bounded, there are no problematic nonlinearities.

To solve these equations, we note that ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} is a linear map from 𝒵m​c"⊗𝒵m​c"→𝒵\mathcal{Z}_{mc}^{\varepsilon}\otimes\mathcal{Z}_{mc}^{\varepsilon}\to\mathcal{Z} and hence we need to solve

It suffices to solve this on the basis 'i"⊗'j"\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{i}^{\varepsilon}\otimes\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{j}^{\varepsilon} consisting of tensor products of eigenvectors 'i\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{i} to ℒ~m​c"\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{mc}^{\varepsilon}. So, equation (3.10) simplifies to solving

Note that this has a solution for all tensors 'i"⊗'j"\varphi_{i}^{\varepsilon}\otimes\varphi_{j}^{\varepsilon} if �i"+�j"\lambda_{i}^{\varepsilon}+\lambda_{j}^{\varepsilon} is in the resolvent set of ℒ~l​c"​( )\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}). The solution has a bound of order one, provided that �i"+�j"\lambda_{i}^{\varepsilon}+\lambda_{j}^{\varepsilon} is uniformly bounded away from the spectrum of ℒ~l​c"​( )\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}). The same argument applies to ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2}, which is a linear map from 𝒵m​c⊗𝒵l​c→𝒵\mathcal{Z}_{mc}\otimes\mathcal{Z}_{lc}\to\mathcal{Z}. So, ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} is defined provided that �i"+�j"\lambda_{i}^{\varepsilon}+\lambda_{j}^{\varepsilon} is in the resolvent set of ℒ~l​c"​( )\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}), where �i"\lambda_{i}^{\varepsilon} is an eigenvalue of ℒ~m​c"​( i)\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{mc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{i}) and �j"\lambda_{j}^{\varepsilon} is an eigenvalue of ℒ~l​c"​( j)\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{j}) where i+ j= \boldsymbol{\gamma}_{i}+\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{j}=\boldsymbol{\gamma}. Then, ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} has an order one bound if �i"+�j"\lambda_{i}^{\varepsilon}+\lambda_{j}^{\varepsilon} is uniformly bounded away from the spectrum of ℒ~l​c"​( )\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}). The same applies to ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3}. However, while such a uniform bound exists for ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} and ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3}, it turns out that we can only obtain an "\varepsilon-dependent lower bound for ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2}. This is in contrast to the one-dimensional case discussed in [HS99], where a uniform bound is obtained. Nevertheless, and due to the specific geometry of the eigenvalues, cf. Figure 4, we still obtain the following result.

Lemma 3.5.

There exist maps ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} and ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3}, which satisfy (3.10) and are bounded independently of "\varepsilon. Additionally, there are maps ℬ2,1\mathcal{B}_{2,1} and ℬ2,2\mathcal{B}_{2,2}, which are bounded independently of "\varepsilon such that

ℬ2=ℬ2,1+"−12​ℬ2,2\mathcal{B}_{2}=\mathcal{B}_{2,1}+\varepsilon^{-\tfrac{1}{2}}\mathcal{B}_{2,2}

is a solution to (3.10).

Before we prove this result, we observe that this is sufficient to choose �>12\beta>\tfrac{1}{2} to guarantee that the normal-form transformation is indeed a near-identity transformation. This does not pose additional challenges to the subsequent centre manifold reduction.

Proof.

For ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} we note that �i"\lambda_{i}^{\varepsilon} and �j"\lambda_{j}^{\varepsilon} as eigenvalues of ℒ~m​c"​( )\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{mc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}) lie in a neighbourhood of size 𝒪⁡(")\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) of the origin. In contrast, the spectrum of ℒ~l​c"​( )\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}) has an imaginary part which is strictly bounded away from zero. This allows us to define ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} with an 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1)-bound.

Similarly, for ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3} we find that the spectrum of ℒ~h"​( )\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{h}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}) is strictly bounded away from the imaginary axis uniformly in "\varepsilon. Therefore, we find a map ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3} with an 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1)-bound.

It remains to construct ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2}. The main issue is that, under the assumption that cot⁡(�)=3​ℚ\cot(\theta)=\sqrt{3}\mathbb{Q}, there exist wave-number pairs 1\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1} and 2\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{2} with | 1− 2|=1|\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1}-\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{2}|=1 such that ℒ~l​c"​( 1)\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1}) and ℒ~l​c"​( 2)\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{2}) have eigenvalues with the same imaginary part for "=0\varepsilon=0, see Remark 3.6. Therefore, we cannot expect to obtain a transformation ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2}, which is bounded as "→0\varepsilon\to 0.

Instead, we split ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} into two parts ℬ2,1\mathcal{B}_{2,1} and ℬ~2,2\tilde{\mathcal{B}}_{2,2}. The first part ℬ2,1\mathcal{B}_{2,1} is constructed to remove all quadratic combinations, where the eigenvalues of ℒ~l​c"​( 1)\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1}) and ℒ~l​c"​( 2)\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{2}) have different imaginary parts at "=0\varepsilon=0. In this case, the existence of a bounded map ℬ2,1\mathcal{B}_{2,1} follows as for ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} and ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3}. In particular ℬ2,1\mathcal{B}_{2,1} is uniformly bounded in ">0\varepsilon>0 and ( 1, 2)(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1},\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{2}). The latter follows from the fact that the eigenvalues of ℒ~0\tilde{\mathcal{L}}^{0}, which lie on the imaginary axis, are discrete and have a positive minimal distance, see Propositions 2.3 and 2.7. The second part deals with the resonant case. The key observation is that, while ℒ~l​c"​( 1)\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1}) and ℒ~l​c"​( 2)\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{lc}^{\varepsilon}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{2}) share one eigenvalue for "=0\varepsilon=0, for ">0\varepsilon>0 they have different real parts. Remark 3.12.

We note that the quadratic, self-interaction and cross-interaction coefficients are the same as in [HJ25]. In addition, they are also consistent with [Doe+03] by noting that in this paper, the quadratic nonlinearity is assumed to be of higher order, while in this paper, we only assume that the quadratic nonlinearity is small at the critical Fourier modes, cf. Assumption B.

Remark 3.16.

The calculation above shows that, although the algebraic manipulations are different, the reduced equations on the centre manifold are, to leading order, the same for c0=ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{0}=c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}) and c0≠ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{0}\neq c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}). Indeed, this is not surprising since the reduced equations can also be obtained from the amplitude equations (1.5) by inserting a travelling-wave ansatz. Since the amplitude equations are derived in the stationary frame, they are independent of the chosen speed for the travelling wave. However, it turns out that the critical speed is still hidden in the dynamics of the reduced equations, which change when c0c_{0} passes through ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}), see Section 4 and Figure 8. Indeed, we observe that fronts at supercritical speeds have a monotone profile, while at subcritical speeds, fronts have an oscillatory leading edge. This is consistent with monostable fronts in reaction-diffusion systems.

4  Analysis of reduced equations and pattern interfaces

We now discuss the dynamics of the reduced equations. Specifically, we consider the existence of equilibria, their stability, and the existence of heteroclinic orbits since these correspond to planar patterns and pattern interfaces in the full system (1.1), respectively. The general strategy is to first analyse the leading-order dynamics given by the truncated system for �∈[0,�6)\theta\in[0,\tfrac{\pi}{6}), which reads as

@�​A1=B1,@�​B1=−�04​(𝐝⋅𝐤1)2​A1−c04​(𝐝⋅𝐤1)2​B1−14​(𝐝⋅𝐤1)2​(�2​A¯2​A¯3+(K0​|A1|2+K2​(|A2|2+|A3|2))​A1),@�​A2=B2,@�​B2=−�04​(𝐝⋅𝐤2)2​A2−c04​(𝐝⋅𝐤2)2​B2−14​(𝐝⋅𝐤2)2​(�2​A¯1​A¯3+(K0​|A2|2+K2​(|A1|2+|A3|2))​A2),@�​A3=B3,@�​B3=−�04​(𝐝⋅𝐤3)2​A3−c04​(𝐝⋅𝐤3)2​B3−14​(𝐝⋅𝐤3)2​(�2​A¯1​A¯2+(K0​|A3|2+K2​(|A1|2+|A2|2))​A3),\begin{split}\partial_{\Xi}A_{1}&=B_{1},\\ \partial_{\Xi}B_{1}&=-\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{1})^{2}}A_{1}-\dfrac{c_{0}}{4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{1})^{2}}B_{1}-\dfrac{1}{4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{1})^{2}}(\beta_{2}\bar{A}_{2}\bar{A}_{3}+(K_{0}|A_{1}|^{2}+K_{2}(|A_{2}|^{2}+|A_{3}|^{2}))A_{1}),\\ \partial_{\Xi}A_{2}&=B_{2},\\ \partial_{\Xi}B_{2}&=-\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{2})^{2}}A_{2}-\dfrac{c_{0}}{4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{2})^{2}}B_{2}-\dfrac{1}{4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{2})^{2}}(\beta_{2}\bar{A}_{1}\bar{A}_{3}+(K_{0}|A_{2}|^{2}+K_{2}(|A_{1}|^{2}+|A_{3}|^{2}))A_{2}),\\ \partial_{\Xi}A_{3}&=B_{3},\\ \partial_{\Xi}B_{3}&=-\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{3})^{2}}A_{3}-\dfrac{c_{0}}{4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{3})^{2}}B_{3}-\dfrac{1}{4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{3})^{2}}(\beta_{2}\bar{A}_{1}\bar{A}_{2}+(K_{0}|A_{3}|^{2}+K_{2}(|A_{1}|^{2}+|A_{2}|^{2}))A_{3}),\\ \end{split} (4.1)

and is obtained by setting "=0\varepsilon=0 in (3.32). Notably, this system is the travelling-wave ODE corresponding to the Ginzburg–Landau system obtained as a formal amplitude system close to a Turing instability, see (1.5). In the analysis, we restrict to real-valued solutions since these are sufficient to describe the dynamics typically observed in experiments. We then show the existence of equilibria in (4.1) corresponding to roll waves, hexagons and mixed modes in (1.1), cf. Corollary 4.1. We note that, as already noticed in equivariant bifurcation theory, these are all possible real-valued equilibria.

To analyse the stability of the equilibria, we show that the stability structure of the linearisation in the spatial system (4.1) can be characterised through the temporal stability of the corresponding equilibria in a system of Landau equations which governs the dynamics of spatially homogeneous solutions to the Ginzburg–Landau system (1.5). Specifically, if an equilibrium is temporally stable, the corresponding equilibrium in the spatial system is a saddle with even splitting between stable and unstable directions. Moreover, a temporally-unstable equilibrium corresponds to a stable equilibrium in the spatial system. Therefore, understanding a three-dimensional eigenvalue problem is sufficient to determine the stability structure in the six-dimensional spatial system.

Subsequently, we discuss the existence of heteroclinic orbits between equilibria analytically. Outside of the invariant subspace of roll waves {A1,B1∈ℝ,A2=B2=A3=B3=0}\{A_{1},B_{1}\in\mathbb{R},A_{2}=B_{2}=A_{3}=B_{3}=0\}, where the leading-order system (4.1) reduces to a damped Duffing oscillator, this requires understanding the dynamics in the full six-dimensional phase space. Exploiting that the leading-order system (4.1) has a strictly decreasing Lyapunov function, for �0>0\mu_{0}>0, we can rigorously show the existence of heteroclinic orbits connecting the non-trivial equilibrium with the lowest energy (either down-hexagons or roll waves) to the trivial equilibrium, which persist in the reduced equations (3.32) for ">0\varepsilon>0. In the pattern-forming system (1.1), these correspond to pattern interfaces, where the spatially homogeneous state is invaded by a planar pattern. Using fast-slow analysis, we then show that these orbits also exist in the reduced system for �=�6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}, which can be interpreted as the slow subsystem of (3.32) as �→�6\theta\to\tfrac{\pi}{6}.

4.1  Equilibria and their stability

4.1.1 Equilibria

First, we consider the equilibria of the reduced equations (4.1) and their stability. We point out that the existence of equilibria does not depend on the direction of the front since equilibria of the reduced equations correspond to steady patterns in the Swift–Hohenberg equation (1.1), which is rotationally invariant. In particular, the results also apply to the leading-order system of the reduced equations (3.37), when �=�6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}. Therefore, equilibria are given as solutions to

4.1.2 Temporal vs. spatial stability

We now discuss the stability of the equilibria listed in Corollary 4.1. For this, we introduce some notation. Let 𝐀=(A1,A2,A3)\mathbf{A}=(A_{1},A_{2},A_{3}) be a solution to (4.2). Then, we denote the linearisation of the corresponding equilibrium (A1,0,A2,0,A3,0)(A_{1},0,A_{2},0,A_{3},0) of the first-order spatial-dynamics system (3.32) by 𝔏⁡(𝐀)\mathfrak{L}(\mathbf{A}). The eigenvalue structure of 𝔏⁡(𝐀)\mathfrak{L}(\mathbf{A}) is characterised by the spectral stability of the equilibrium as a solution to the system of Landau equations

@T​A1=�0​A1+�2​A¯2​A¯3+(K0​|A1|2+K2​(|A2|2+|A3|2))​A1,@T​A2=�0​A2+�2​A¯1​A¯3+(K0​|A2|2+K2​(|A1|2+|A3|2))​A2,@T​A3=�0​A3+�2​A¯1​A¯2+(K0​|A3|2+K2​(|A1|2+|A2|2))​A3,\begin{split}\partial_{T}A_{1}&=\mu_{0}A_{1}+\beta_{2}\bar{A}_{2}\bar{A}_{3}+(K_{0}|A_{1}|^{2}+K_{2}(|A_{2}|^{2}+|A_{3}|^{2}))A_{1},\\ \partial_{T}A_{2}&=\mu_{0}A_{2}+\beta_{2}\bar{A}_{1}\bar{A}_{3}+(K_{0}|A_{2}|^{2}+K_{2}(|A_{1}|^{2}+|A_{3}|^{2}))A_{2},\\ \partial_{T}A_{3}&=\mu_{0}A_{3}+\beta_{2}\bar{A}_{1}\bar{A}_{2}+(K_{0}|A_{3}|^{2}+K_{2}(|A_{1}|^{2}+|A_{2}|^{2}))A_{3},\end{split} (4.5)

which is the system of amplitude equations (1.5) without the spatial derivatives. Note that since the (degenerate) diffusion operator in (1.5) is diagonal, spectral stability in (4.5) implies spectral stability in (1.5). Therefore, we refer to this as PDE stability. The following lemma then relates the PDE stability of an equilibrium to its stability in the leading-order system (4.1) on the centre manifold. This relation was already noted in [Doe+03], and we provide a proof for completeness.

Lemma 4.4.

If the linearisation of the Landau equations (4.5) has nn unstable eigenvalues with 0⩽n⩽30\leqslant n\leqslant 3 and 3−n3-n stable eigenvalues, the linearisation of the spatial-dynamics system 𝔏⁡(𝐀)\mathfrak{L}(\mathbf{A}) has 3+n3+n stable eigenvalues and 3−n3-n unstable eigenvalues. Remark 4.5.

The proof of Lemma 4.4 shows that the assumption c0>0c_{0}>0 plays a crucial role for the eigenvalue-structure of 𝔏⁡(𝐀)\mathfrak{L}(\mathbf{A}). In particular, in the case c0<0c_{0}<0 we find that the eigenvalues of 𝔏⁡(𝐀)\mathfrak{L}(\mathbf{A}) cross from stable to unstable (instead from unstable to stable) as 𝐀\mathbf{A} becomes PDE-unstable. In particular, if 𝐀\mathbf{A} is fully PDE-unstable, i.e. ℒGL​(𝐀)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GL}}(\mathbf{A}) has only unstable eigenvalues, then (A1,0,A2,0,A3)(A_{1},0,A_{2},0,A_{3}) is an unstable equilibrium in the leading-order system (4.1).

4.1.3 Stability of equilibria

As motivated above, Lemmas 4.4 and 4.8 allow for a simpler characterisation of the eigenvalue structure of the linearisation in the leading-order system (4.1). From this, we make the immediate observation that the eigenvalue structure does not depend on the direction 𝐝\mathbf{d}. To obtain more detailed information about the stability structure of the equilibria in Corollary 4.1, we now consider their linearisation in the Landau system (4.5).

We recall that the linearisation in the Landau system (4.5) about an equilibrium 𝐀\mathbf{A}, denoted as above by ℒGL​(𝐀)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GL}}(\mathbf{A}), is given by (4.7). First, we note that ℒGL​(𝐀T)=�0​I\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GL}}(\mathbf{A}_{T})=\mu_{0}I is diagonal. Therefore, for �0<0\mu_{0}<0, the corresponding equilibrium in the spatial-dynamics system is a saddle with 3 stable and 3 unstable eigenvalues, whereas for �0>0\mu_{0}>0 it is a stable equilibrium. More specifically, the quadratic eigenvalue problem decouples into three independent equations, given by

0=4(𝐝⋅𝐤j)2�2+c0�+�0,j=1,2,3.0=4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{j})^{2}\lambda^{2}+c_{0}\lambda+\mu_{0},\quad j=1,2,3. (4.13)

This implies that the eigenvalues of 𝔏⁡(𝐀𝔗)\mathfrak{L}(\mathbf{A}_{T}) are real for all c0>ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{0}>c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}). As c0c_{0} decreases through ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}), two eigenvalues collide and then split into a pair of complex-conjugate eigenvalues. In particular, this changes the qualitative dynamics of orbits close to the trivial equilibrium. For c0>ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{0}>c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}) for all j=1,2,3j=1,2,3, orbits decay into the trivial state monotonically, whereas for c0<ccrit​(𝐤j)c_{0}<c_{\mathrm{crit}}(\mathbf{k}_{j}), the trivial equilibrium is a stable centre and oscillations occur, see Figure 8. This is well-known in the one-dimensional case, see e.g. [Hil20], and similar behaviour occurs for other monostable fronts, for example, in the Fisher–KPP equation [SU17, Sec. 7.1].

4.2  Analytic construction of some heteroclinic orbits

We recall from the beginning of this section that our goal is to construct heteroclinic orbits in the leading-order system (4.1), which correspond to planar pattern interfaces in the full problem (1.1). We note that since (4.1) has a six-dimensional phase space, understanding its global dynamics analytically is a non-trivial problem. Therefore, we present here selected orbits that can be constructed using well-understood analytical methods. While it might be possible to obtain a deeper understanding using topological methods such as Conley index theory, see e.g. [MM02], this is beyond the scope of this paper.

We restrict the following analysis to the parameter set �2⩾0\beta_{2}\geqslant 0, K0<0K_{0}<0 and K2<0K_{2}<0, for which we obtain a bifurcation diagram as in Figure 9 and which is also found in [Doe+03] where �2>0\beta_{2}>0, K0=−3K_{0}=-3 and K2=−6K_{2}=-6. Additionally, we restrict to the case �∈(0,�6)\theta\in(0,\tfrac{\pi}{6}) and note that the results can be extended to the case �=�6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6} using the fast-slow analysis presented in Section 4.4.

We first note that {A1,B1∈ℝ,A2=B2=A3=B3=0}\{A_{1},B_{1}\in\mathbb{R},A_{2}=B_{2}=A_{3}=B_{3}=0\} is an invariant subspace of the leading-order reduced equations (4.1), which contains roll waves. In fact, it is an invariant subspace including the higher-order terms in (3.32) due to Remark 3.13. In this space, the reduced equations on the centre manifold simplify to

@�​A1=B1,@�​B1=−�04​(𝐝⋅𝐤1)2​A1−c04​(𝐝⋅𝐤1)2​B1−K0​A134​(𝐝⋅𝐤1)2,\begin{split}\partial_{\Xi}A_{1}&=B_{1},\\ \partial_{\Xi}B_{1}&=-\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{1})^{2}}A_{1}-\dfrac{c_{0}}{4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{1})^{2}}B_{1}-\dfrac{K_{0}A_{1}^{3}}{4(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{1})^{2}},\end{split}

which is the first-order formulation of a homogeneous, damped Duffing oscillator. For this system, when �0>0\mu_{0}>0, heteroclinic orbits connecting the non-trivial equilibrium to the trivial equilibrium can be constructed via a straightforward phase-plane analysis, see Figure 10.

While in the case 𝐝=(1,0)\mathbf{d}=(1,0) there is another invariant subspace {A2=A3 and B2=B3}\{A_{2}=A_{3}\text{ and }B_{2}=B_{3}\}, this is not invariant for any other 𝐝\mathbf{d} with �∈(0,�6)\theta\in(0,\tfrac{\pi}{6}) since (𝐝⋅𝐤2)2≠(𝐝⋅𝐤3)2(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{2})^{2}\neq(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{3})^{2}. Even in the case 𝐝=(1,0)\mathbf{d}=(1,0), the phase space is still four-dimensional. Nevertheless, we are still able to construct selected heteroclinic orbits analytically. Since the construction works the same way, we directly consider the full leading-order system (4.1) for general directions 𝐝\mathbf{d} and prove that for any c0>0c_{0}>0 there exists a heteroclinic orbit connecting either down-hexagons 𝐀H−\mathbf{A}_{H_{-}} or roll waves 𝐀R\mathbf{A}_{R} to the trivial state 𝐀T\mathbf{A}_{T} depending on the parameter values (�0,K0,K2)(\mu_{0},K_{0},K_{2}).

The main observation for the analysis is that the leading-order system (4.1) has a Lyapunov function given by

ℋ⁡(𝐀,𝐁)=Xj=13⁡2​(𝐝⋅𝐤j)2​|Bj|2+�02​Xj=13⁡|Aj|2+�2​A1​A2​A3+K04​Xj=13⁡|Aj|4+K22​(A12​A22+A12​A32+A22​A32).\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B})=\sum_{j=1}^{3}2(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{j})^{2}|B_{j}|^{2}+\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{3}|A_{j}|^{2}+\beta_{2}A_{1}A_{2}A_{3}+\dfrac{K_{0}}{4}\sum_{j=1}^{3}|A_{j}|^{4}+\dfrac{K_{2}}{2}(A_{1}^{2}A_{2}^{2}+A_{1}^{2}A_{3}^{2}+A_{2}^{2}A_{3}^{2}). (4.14)

Indeed, a direct calculation gives that along a solution (𝐀⁡(�),𝐁⁡(�))(\mathbf{A}(\Xi),\mathbf{B}(\Xi))

@�​ℋ​(𝐀⁡(�),𝐁⁡(�))=−c0​|𝐁⁡(�)|2⩽0.\partial_{\Xi}\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{A}(\Xi),\mathbf{B}(\Xi))=-c_{0}|\mathbf{B}(\Xi)|^{2}\leqslant 0. (4.15)

From this, we note that for c0>0c_{0}>0, the Lyapunov function ℋ\mathcal{H} is strictly decreasing along non-stationary solutions. For c0=0c_{0}=0, we find that ℋ\mathcal{H} is conserved along solutions. In fact, the leading-order system (4.1) is a Hamiltonian system with Hamiltonian ℋ\mathcal{H}. This observation can be used to show that there exist �H+↔T<0\mu_{H_{+}\leftrightarrow T}<0 and �H+↔R>0\mu_{H_{+}\leftrightarrow R}>0 and corresponding reversible heteroclinic orbits in (4.1) from 𝐀H+\mathbf{A}_{H_{+}} to 𝐀T\mathbf{A}_{T} and 𝐀H+\mathbf{A}_{H_{+}} to 𝐀R\mathbf{A}_{R}, respectively, using variational techniques for Hamiltonian systems, see e.g. [Ste08]. However, we note that the centre manifold analysis in Theorem 3.10 does not apply for c0=0c_{0}=0. While a spatial centre manifold approach, see e.g. [HS12], can be used to construct a centre manifold in the case c0=0c_{0}=0, the resulting manifold can be of arbitrary dimension depending on the direction 𝐝\mathbf{d}. Although the leading-order system is expected to have an invariant manifold where the dynamics are given by (3.32), this does not extend to the full centre manifold. In particular, due to the presence of highly oscillatory higher-order terms, the persistence of the orbits is non-trivial. We plan to treat this problem in a future paper.

Using the Lyapunov function, we now construct heteroclinic orbits for �0>0\mu_{0}>0 and c0>0c_{0}>0. The construction uses the following strategy. Let 𝐀`\mathbf{A}_{\ell} be the non-trivial equilibrium with the lowest energy. Note here that since �0>0\mu_{0}>0, the trivial equilibrium is stable due to Lemma 4.4. Thus, the corresponding stable manifold is six-dimensional. Moreover, we show that (𝐀`,𝟎)∈@​ (\mathbf{A}_{\ell},\mathbf{0})\in\partial\Omega. Remark 4.11.

We point out that the proof of Theorem 4.10 in particular shows that \Omega is uniformly bounded in 𝐝\mathbf{d}.

Before considering the persistence of the orbits established in Theorem 4.10, we briefly discuss the existence of other heteroclinic orbits. A fully rigorous construction of such orbits is highly non-trivial due to the high-dimensional phase space and the lack of symmetries, which prevents a direct further reduction to smaller invariant subspaces, with the exception of the invariant subspace containing roll waves as the only non-trivial pattern. However, we conjecture, for example, the existence of heteroclinic orbits connecting the other non-trivial equilibria to the trivial one, as well as a heteroclinic orbit connecting up-hexagons to roll waves for �0>0\mu_{0}>0 before the bifurcation of the mixed modes from the roll waves. In the fast-front case treated in [HJ25], such orbits can be found rigorously using phase plane analysis. Here, the former orbits can be found using a numerical shooting algorithm, see Figure 1 for an invasion of up-hexagons into the trivial state and Figures 12a and 12b for an invasion of mixed modes and false hexagons into the trivial state. The construction of the latter orbit is difficult even numerically, and we leave a detailed numerical analysis for future research. However, by performing systematic shooting in directions of the unstable manifold of the equilibrium corresponding to up-hexagons, we find orbits that connect to the trivial equilibrium but come close to the roll-wave equilibrium. The corresponding pattern interface is a two-stage invasion of up-hexagons into the trivial state with a large plateau of roll waves as an intermediate state, see Figure 12c. As discussed in Section 1.2, this is a typical mechanism of how hexagons arise in experiments.

4.3  Persistence of heteroclinic orbits

We now discuss the persistence of heteroclinic orbits in the leading-order system (4.1) as solutions to the full reduced equation on the centre manifold (3.32). For this, we first note that the equilibria obtained in Corollary 4.1 are hyperbolic outside of bifurcation points and therefore, as discussed in [HJ25], the bifurcation diagram persists. Next, for �0>0\mu_{0}>0, we consider heteroclinic orbits in the leading-order system (4.1), which connect a non-trivial equilibrium (𝐀`,𝟎)(\mathbf{A}_{\ell},\mathbf{0}) to the trivial equilibrium (𝐀T,𝟎)(\mathbf{A}_{T},\mathbf{0}). For this, we note the heteroclinic orbit lies in both the stable manifold of (𝐀T,𝟎)(\mathbf{A}_{T},\mathbf{0}) and the unstable manifold of (𝐀`,𝟎)(\mathbf{A}_{\ell},\mathbf{0}) and thus, they intersect. Since the stable manifold of the trivial equilibrium (𝐀T,𝟎)(\mathbf{A}_{T},\mathbf{0}) is a six-dimensional manifold in ℝ6\mathbb{R}^{6}, this intersection is transversal and persists under perturbation. This yields the following result.

Theorem 4.12.

Let �0\mu_{0} and �∈(0,�6)\theta\in(0,\tfrac{\pi}{6}) with cot⁡(�)∈3​ℚ\cot(\theta)\in\sqrt{3}\mathbb{Q}. Any heteroclinic orbit of the leading-order system (4.1), which connects to the trivial equilibrium, persists as a solution to the full reduced equation (3.32). In particular, the heteroclinic orbits constructed in Theorem 4.10 persist.

We point out that the persistence of other heteroclinic orbits, which do not connect to the trivial state, is less obvious. For example, we consider a potential connection between up-hexagons and roll waves for �0>0\mu_{0}>0 before the bifurcation of mixed modes from the roll waves. Recalling the dimensions of the respective stable and unstable manifolds depicted in Figure 9, we find that, in this regime, the unstable manifold of the up-hexagons is three-dimensional and the stable manifold of the roll waves is four-dimensional (since the equilibria are hyperbolic). Therefore, we must show that the intersection of a three-dimensional manifold with a four-dimensional manifold persists in a six-dimensional phase space. Counting dimensions, the intersections between these manifolds will generically be transversal and thus persistent. However, to the best of our knowledge, there is no general result that excludes the occurrence of degenerate situations in which the intersection is not transversal. Therefore, the persistence of such orbits, even if they can be constructed in the leading-order system, remains an open question.

5  Pattern interfaces on a square lattice

So far, the construction was restricted to patterns which lie on a hexagonal Fourier lattice generated by 𝐤1\mathbf{k}_{1}, 𝐤2\mathbf{k}_{2} and 𝐤3\mathbf{k}_{3} given in (1.3). Notably, this lattice does not support square patterns, which are generated by the Fourier wave vectors 𝐤1=(1,0)\mathbf{k}_{1}=(1,0) and 𝐤2=(0,1)\mathbf{k}_{2}=(0,1). Therefore, we now discuss how to obtain pattern interfaces on this square Fourier lattice �□\Gamma_{\square}. Since the construction largely follows that of the hexagonal lattice and is significantly easier because the square lattice is non-resonant, we only report the differences. In particular, the full analysis can be carried out without using Assumption B.

5.1  Spectral analysis

Consider now a direction 𝐝=(cos⁡(�),sin⁡(�))∈S1\mathbf{d}=(\cos(\theta),\sin(\theta))\in S^{1} with �∈[0,�4)\theta\in[0,\tfrac{\pi}{4}). We reiterate that it is sufficient to consider only 0⩽�<�40\leqslant\theta<\tfrac{\pi}{4} since all other angles can be obtained by using the D4D_{4}-symmetry of (1.1). We note that the ansatz (1.9) and the resulting spatial dynamics formulation (1.11) do not depend on the specific choice of Fourier lattice and therefore, do not change. Similarly, the geometric interpretation of the eigenvalue problem given by Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2 is unchanged, see Figure 13. A direct consequence of the geometric interpretation of the spectrum is that a more-central Jordan block of size four now occurs for �=0\theta=0 instead of �=�6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6} since 𝐤2⟂(1,0)\mathbf{k}_{2}\perp(1,0). Therefore, Proposition 2.3 holds verbatim with the condition �=�6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6} replaced by �=0\theta=0. Next, we note that the angle condition for the presence of a spectral gap given in Proposition 2.4 changes from cot⁡(�)∈3​ℚ\cot(\theta)\in\sqrt{3}\mathbb{Q} to cot⁡(�)∈ℚ\cot(\theta)\in\mathbb{Q}, which follows from the same algebraic computations using that 𝐝⟂⋅ =−n1​sin⁡(�)+n2​cos⁡(�)\mathbf{d}^{\perp}\cdot\boldsymbol{\gamma}=-n_{1}\sin(\theta)+n_{2}\cos(\theta) for =n1​𝐤1+n2​𝐤2∈�□\boldsymbol{\gamma}=n_{1}\mathbf{k}_{1}+n_{2}\mathbf{k}_{2}\in\Gamma_{\square}. To conclude the spectral analysis, we find that there are eight more-central eigenvalues (for �≠0\theta\neq 0) or six (for �=0\theta=0) which still have the expansions (2.6) and (2.7), respectively. The remaining statements of Lemmas 2.5 and 2.6 and Proposition 2.7 hold unchanged under the angle condition cot⁡(�)∈ℚ\cot(\theta)\in\mathbb{Q}.

5.2  Centre manifold theory and reduced equations

In the centre manifold theory, we first remark that the functional-analytic setup is independent of a specific choice of Fourier lattice, and thus holds unchanged. The projections can then be defined in the same way, and the estimates in Lemma 3.3 hold with the natural changes to the angle. We then define the splitting of WW into more-central, less-central, and hyperbolic parts as in (3.6) and introduce the same rescaled variables (3.7), as well as the resulting system (3.8).

The main change compared to the hexagonal case is in the following normal-form analysis. First, since the square lattice is non-resonant, we find 𝒫m​c"​(𝐤j)​𝒩^​("�​W ^m​c,𝐤j,#)=0\mathcal{P}_{mc}^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{k}_{j})\hat{\mathcal{N}}(\varepsilon^{\beta}\underaccent{\vphantom{W}\smash{\raisebox{1.59735pt}{\kern 0.0pt\rule{5.58054pt}{0.6pt}}}}{\hat{W}}_{mc};\mathbf{k}_{j},\vartheta)=0. In particular, this implies that Assumption B is not necessary in the square case. Second, we find that in 𝒩 ^l​c​(W ^m​c,W ^l​c+W ^h, ,#)\underaccent{\vphantom{W}\smash{\raisebox{1.59735pt}{\kern 0.0pt\rule{5.58054pt}{0.6pt}}}}{\hat{\mathcal{N}}}_{lc}(\underaccent{\vphantom{W}\smash{\raisebox{1.59735pt}{\kern 0.0pt\rule{5.58054pt}{0.6pt}}}}{\hat{W}}_{mc},\underaccent{\vphantom{W}\smash{\raisebox{1.59735pt}{\kern 0.0pt\rule{5.58054pt}{0.6pt}}}}{\hat{W}}_{lc}+\underaccent{\vphantom{W}\smash{\raisebox{1.59735pt}{\kern 0.0pt\rule{5.58054pt}{0.6pt}}}}{\hat{W}}_{h};\boldsymbol{\gamma},\vartheta) the same problematic nonlinearities appear. Therefore, we make the near-identity transformation, which is still given by (3.9) and results in the equations (3.10) for ℬ1,ℬ2,ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{1},\mathcal{B}_{2},\mathcal{B}_{3}. While we obtain a 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1)-bound for ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} and ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3} already in the hexagonal case, ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} did not have a uniform bound due to the resonance of the hexagonal lattice, cf. Lemma 3.5 and Figure 5. This simplifies in the square case since there are no two lattice points in �□\Gamma_{\square} that generate less-central eigenvalues with the same imaginary part and have distance one. Therefore, we find that ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} is also uniformly bounded as "→0\varepsilon\to 0.

With this normal-form transformation, Lemma 3.7 holds unchanged, and in particular, the nonlinearities in the transformed equations satisfy the Lipschitz bounds (3.13) with the same scaling in "\varepsilon. Additionally, the semigroup bounds hold unchanged after replacing the angle condition with cot⁡(�)∈ℚ\cot(\theta)\in\mathbb{Q} and distinguishing the case �=0\theta=0. Therefore, we obtain a centre manifold theorem as in Theorem 3.10 for �≠0\theta\neq 0 and Theorem 3.15 for �=0\theta=0. 6  Discussion

In this paper, we construct slow-moving pattern interfaces with general spreading direction in a two-dimensional Swift–Hohenberg-type equation. These interfaces describe the invasion of a linearly unstable, spatially homogeneous state by either roll waves or planar hexagonal patterns. We also present evidence for the existence of two-stage invasion processes, where the homogeneous state is first invaded by roll waves, which in turn are invaded by hexagonal patterns through a secondary front interface.

We conclude this discussion with a brief overview of related questions and potential pathways for further investigation.

Front selection

While it is well-understood that planar patterns, specifically hexagonal patterns, arise through planar or radial pattern interfaces, the exact mechanism is not understood rigorously. In the spatially one-dimensional case, some rigorous selection results are available. In particular, for fronts in reaction-diffusion equations such as the Fisher–KPP equation, a rigorous theory for the selected speed has been developed recently, and we refer to [AS22] and to the recent overview [AHS25]. Moreover, rigorous selection results for pattern-forming fronts specifically have only been obtained very recently [ACR26]. However, in the two-dimensional case considered here, many open problems remain regarding (a) the selected invasion speed and (b) the selected pattern in the wake when starting from a compactly supported perturbation of the linearly unstable trivial state.

The two-dimensional situation is even more complicated since, in experiments, the selection of planar patterns is facilitated through a cascade of invading fronts, which typically do not travel with the same speed. An example for this is that the hexagonal pattern in thermal convection typically forms as a secondary invasion to roll waves, which are the selected pattern in the leading edge of the front [PN94, CM99]. The main challenge in understanding these structures rigorously is the fact that the connecting state is unstable and that the amplitude solution is not a travelling wave. This is an open question even for one-dimensional reaction-diffusion systems, and we refer to [GH25] for first linear stability results.

Rigorous heteroclinics

While we construct selected heteroclinic orbits analytically in Section 4.2, these only cover parts of the orbits that we find numerically, cf. Figures 1, 2 and 12. Specifically, the rigorous existence of two-stage invasion processes corresponding to heteroclinic orbits from up-hexagons to the trivial state that pass close to the roll waves remains open. The main problem is that the phase space of the reduced equations is still six-dimensional, which makes any global analysis challenging even though the reduced equations have a strictly decreasing Lyapunov function. The partial results of this paper rely on the observation that the energy landscape is topologically very simple close to the trivial equilibrium allowing for the construction of a sufficiently large trapping region that has an intersection with the unstable manifold of the non-trivial equilibrium with the lowest energy. Beyond that trapping region, the energy landscape is topologically more complicated and more involved methods have to be used. One such topological method to construct heteroclinic orbits is Conley index theory [Con78, MM02], which has already been mentioned in [Doe+03] as a potential pathway.

Extending the set of allowed angles

The construction of planar interfaces in the paper is restricted to directions satisfying the condition cot⁡(�)∈3​ℚ\cot(\theta)\in\sqrt{3}\mathbb{Q}, which guarantees the existence of a spectral gap around the imaginary axis at "=0\varepsilon=0, see Proposition 2.4. The case cot⁡(�)∉3​ℚ\cot(\theta)\notin\sqrt{3}\mathbb{Q} is much more challenging since there exists a sequence of hyperbolic eigenvalues which accumulate at the imaginary axis at infinity. This suggests the presence of a small-divisor problem, which could potentially be solved using Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser (KAM) theory to obtain pattern interfaces in directions satisfying a Diophantine condition. However, we expect that this is a technical challenge and that the reduced dynamics to leading order are still given by (1.6) obtained from the amplitude equations. Nevertheless, the proof of this remains an open problem.

Data availability statement

The explicit computations for the front speed via a marginal stability analysis were performed using Mathematica [Mat]. The numerical simulations of orbits in the leading-order system (4.1) were done using Julia [Bez+17]. This was also used to plot the pattern interfaces using the leading-order expressions in Theorem 4.14 with the numerically obtained amplitudes. Finally, the simulations of the selected front speeds presented in Appendix B were done using FEniCSx [Bar+23]. The code used to generate the corresponding data is available under [HJ26].

The equation (B.1) is recast as the second-order system

@t​u=�​u−�​|∇u|2−u3−w−�​w,w=u+�​u\begin{split}\partial_{t}u&=\mu u-\beta|\nabla u|^{2}-u^{3}-w-\Delta w,\\ w&=u+\Delta u\end{split}

in a mixed finite-element formulation, and then discretised with continuous piecewise-linear finite elements on an unstructured triangular mesh with 1884×3261884\times 326 mesh points, which is a spatial resolution of �​x=115\Delta x=\tfrac{1}{15}. The time-discretisation is then done using a Crank-Nicolson scheme with fixed time step �​t=150\Delta t=\frac{1}{50} over T=100T=100 time units. The resulting nonlinear system at each step is solved with Newton–Raphson line search with residual tolerance of 10−1010^{-10}. The implementation uses the FEniCSx software stack (DOLFINx/UFL/Basix) for weak-form assembly and mesh management, with PETSc providing the linear algebra backend and nonlinear solver; see [Bar+23].

Since we are interested in planar fronts, we choose the initial condition

u0​(𝐱)="​(Xj=13⁡Ahex​cos⁡(𝐤j⋅𝐱))​1−tanh⁡(𝐱⋅𝐝−'`)2\displaystyle u_{0}(\mathbf{x})=\varepsilon\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{3}A_{\mathrm{hex}}\cos(\mathbf{k}_{j}\cdot\mathbf{x})\Bigr)\frac{1-\tanh(\tfrac{\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{d}-\varphi}{\ell})}{2}

with a localisation width `=3\ell=3 and amplitude

Ahex=−�2−�22−4​�0​(K0+2​K2)2​(K0+2​K2),\displaystyle A_{\mathrm{hex}}=\frac{-\beta_{2}-\sqrt{\beta_{2}^{2}-4\mu_{0}(K_{0}+2K_{2})}}{2(K_{0}+2K_{2})},

which imposes a steep profile in direction 𝐝=(cos⁡(�),sin⁡(�))\mathbf{d}=(\cos(\theta),\sin(\theta)) connecting hexagons to the spatially homogeneous state. For the choice of parameters, we expect hexagons to be stable with respect to all other stationary patterns: indeed, for (B.1) it holds K0=−3K_{0}=-3 and K2=−6K_{2}=-6, cf. [Doe+03], and with �0=1\mu_{0}=1 we are in the regime before the bifurcation of the mixed-mode branch in Figure 9. We consider two initial profiles: the first for angle �=0\theta=0 and the second for an angle �=�6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}. Note that we shift the second initial condition to the right by setting '=2​�\varphi=2\pi to make sure no boundary effects from the left-hand boundary affect the dynamics.

The front position xf​(t)x_{f}(t) is then determined by tracking the L2L^{2}-norm of a rolling 2​�2\pi-wide strip in front direction and defining xf​(t)x_{f}(t) to be the rightmost position, where this norm exceeds the threshold �=0.052\delta=\frac{0.05}{\sqrt{2}}. From the discussion of the selected front speed in Section 1.2, cf. (1.8), we obtain the linearly predicted speed

cpred​(�)=4​"​(1−(𝐝⟂⋅𝐤1)2)​�0,\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{pred}}(\theta)=4\varepsilon\sqrt{(1-(\mathbf{d}^{\perp}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{1})^{2})\mu_{0}},

where 𝐝⟂=(−sin⁡(�),cos⁡(�))⟂𝐝\mathbf{d}^{\perp}=(-\sin(\theta),\cos(\theta))\perp\mathbf{d}. Inserting the parameters gives the predicted front speeds

cpred​(0)=1.2andcpred​(�6)≈1.039.\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{pred}}(0)=1.2\quad\text{and}\quad c_{\mathrm{pred}}(\tfrac{\pi}{6})\approx 1.039.

Since we expect a relaxation of the initial condition to the selected front profile and hence a relaxation of the front speed, we fit a linear curve to xf​(t)x_{f}(t) in the interval [t0,t1][t_{0},t_{1}]. Note that we also restrict from above as the plots indicate boundary effects on the right-hand-side boundary to affect the front. For �=0\theta=0, the front speed has relaxed at t0=20t_{0}=20 and boundary effects are visible after t1=80t_{1}=80, while for �=�6\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6} the front settles at t0=30t_{0}=30 and boundary effects are visible at t1=80t_{1}=80. With this curve, we find the numerical front speeds

cnum​(0)≈1.1134andcnum​(�6)=0.9922\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{num}}(0)\approx 1.1134\quad\text{and}\quad c_{\mathrm{num}}(\tfrac{\pi}{6})=0.9922

being a reasonable match for the predicted front speed, with a relative error of approximately 7.2%7.2\% and 4.5%4.5\% respectively. The remaining discrepancy is consistent with logarithmic corrections of the position not captured by the leading-order marginal stability prediction, which lead to a correction of the front speed of order 1t\tfrac{1}{t}. These corrections have been rigorously found in monostable fronts in reaction-diffusion systems, see [AHS25]. We also observe that the leading edge of the front exhibits a stripe-like structure before the pattern settles into the hexagonal bulk state, see Figures 20 and 21. This is consistent with experimental observations, see e.g. [PN94, CM99].

The data of the front speeds is shown in Figure 19, and snapshots of the solutions at selected times are shown in Figure 20.
